Senses.Explanation: As part of the stable labels 'Baizhang's wild fox' (百丈野狐), 'the wild-fox story' (野狐話), and 'the wild-fox public case' (野狐公案), the word names the public case attached to Baizhang. Masters raise, debate, and versify this case. Its recorded hinge is the contrast between 'does not fall under cause and effect' (不落因果) and 'is not blind to cause and effect' (不昧因果). This is a named lexical object, not the animal body inside its narrative and not a person rebuked as a wild-fox spirit.
Senses.Note: Primary Zen-loaded sense. The corpus bends an animal name into a stable case-name, explicitly marking it with 'raise' (舉), 'story' (話), and 'public case' (公案).

Occurrences.Kwic: 師室中常舉百丈野狐話問僧，對者多不契。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The master repeatedly raises Baizhang's wild-fox story in the chamber to question monks, explicitly deploying it as a named case.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂，舉百丈野狐話，乃曰：不是翻濤手，徒誇跨海鯨。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In a hall address the master raises Baizhang's wild-fox story and comments on it, again treating the phrase as a case-title.

Senses.Explanation: The concrete transformed animal body within the Baizhang account. The old man says that an answer of 'does not fall under cause and effect' led to five hundred births in a wild-fox body; after Baizhang answers 'is not blind to cause and effect,' the old man reports release from that body. Later records debate whether either formula leaves, produces, or releases the wild-fox body. Those debates still refer to the narrative body and do not turn each reading of the exchange into another sense.
Senses.Note: Literal narrative referent. It remains separate from the case as a textual object and from the abusive wild-fox-spirit label.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不落因果。遂五百生墮野狐身
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Baizhang account connects the answer 'does not fall under cause and effect' with five hundred births in a wild-fox body.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不昧囙果老人於言下大悟告辝師云某甲已免野狐身
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After Baizhang says 'is not blind to cause and effect,' the old man reports release from the wild-fox body.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不昧因果，也未脫得野狐身。一云：不落因果，又何曾墮野狐來
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Two monks explicitly debate the two formulas through the continued or denied wild-fox body.

Senses.Explanation: As 'wild-fox spirit' (野狐精), the word forms an abusive epithet for a person or view. Masters shout it at interlocutors, and Dahui warns against making a 'wild-fox-spirit interpretation' (野狐精見解). The referent is the person or understanding being denounced, not the animal body in the Baizhang narrative or the case as a textual object.
Senses.Note: The distinct referent is established by direct address and by the evaluative compound for an interpretation.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: A master rebukes an interlocutor directly as 'this wild-fox spirit.'
Dahui rejects treating the matter as a wild-fox-spirit interpretation.

Senses.Explanation: Literally "wild fox" (野狐) plus "Chan" (禪): "wild-fox Chan," attested 16 times in 15 allowlisted texts. It is an adverse label within the Chinese Chan record, applied to claims, verbal display, or conduct that the speaker rejects as counterfeit or distorted Chan. Liao'an praises lines whose every sound "tears apart wild-fox Chan" (聲聲裂破野狐禪) and elsewhere says to "painstakingly sweep away wild-fox Chan" (痛掃野狐禪). Ruibai calls it "wild-fox Chan from various quarters" (諸方野狐禪) when criticizing attempts to define a lineage from Bodhidharma's reply to Emperor Wu, "really, no merit" (實無功德). Fangrong, after a monk shouts and then has no reply, asks, "what tricks is wild-fox Chan showing off?" (野狐禪逞甚伎倆).
Senses.Note: The label is related by wording to the Baizhang wild-fox case (百丈野狐), but the corpus does not restrict it to citations of that case. Its verbs are openly corrective: "tear apart" (裂破), "sweep away" (掃), and "show off tricks" (逞伎倆). A verse placed under the Baizhang case says, "a whole troop carries on wild-fox Chan; over five hundred lives, one saying comes round" (修行一隊野狐禪，五百生來一語圓). The verse's own narrative language is retained as a recorded case allusion and not generalized beyond that witness.

Occurrences.Kwic: 句句盡同師子吼，聲聲裂破野狐禪。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Liao'an's verse says, "each sentence is entirely like a lion's roar; each sound tears apart wild-fox Chan." Liao'an has no exact project-roster link.

Occurrences.Kwic: 諸方野狐禪以達磨對梁王實無功德一語
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Ruibai criticizes "wild-fox Chan from various quarters" that takes Bodhidharma's one reply to the Liang emperor, "really, no merit," as a lineage label. Ruibai has no safe exact roster link.
After a monk shouts and then gives no answer, the teacher says, "what tricks is wild-fox Chan showing off?" The record's teacher has no safe exact roster link.

Occurrences.Kwic: 修行一隊野狐禪，五百生來一語圓。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse under the Baizhang wild-fox case says, "a whole troop carries on wild-fox Chan; over five hundred lives, one saying comes round." This is a later verse on a raised case, not a safely linkable speaker turn.
A portrait verse says its subject "sweeps away all the wild-fox Chan of the various quarters." The verse heading does not supply a safe roster identity for the described subject.
